old_entry.title: MUD
old_entry.subtitle: A world made of words, inhabited together
old_entry.summary: Roy Trubshaw and Richard Bartle helped make the computer terminal a meeting place.
body: Roy Trubshaw began MUD at the University of Essex in 1978; Richard Bartle became a central collaborator as the project evolved. The name stood for Multi-User Dungeon. Instead of merely reading a description, participants could act in a shared textual space and encounter one another.

MUDs linked adventure-game commands to persistent social worlds. Their descendants include online role-playing games, but their significance is broader: a world can feel inhabited through language and other people, even without a moving image.

editorial_features.title: Who shares the dark?
body: Roy Trubshaw's first MUD at Essex was a small collection of connected places where people could move and talk. In his 1990 history, Richard Bartle distinguishes it from the better-known BCPL rewrite completed around Easter 1980. An intervening version let people add rooms and commands during play, but unrestricted additions could undermine exploration and the world's coherence. Openness created a design problem, not an automatic community. The program needed a way to let several people inhabit it without every new command unmaking what others had come to explore.

A shared room also needed shared consequences. Bartle recalled an early anomaly: one person's torch did not let the other person see. Adding containers, inhabitants and scoring meant making the world's rules work across participants, rather than copying a solitary adventure for several users. Even elevated authority grew from a tool: the designers' debugging mode became the power available to experienced wizards. The same machinery that helped an author inspect a new area could later change a player's relationship to everyone else inside it.

Bartle's March 1985 magazine account describes what that authority allowed. A wizard could watch another player's screen without their knowledge through a feature originally intended to expose usability problems. The account treats the resulting spectatorship as entertainment and an incentive to progress. Reading it now raises a specific question about consent, rather than proving that all early players agreed on privacy. A world made from text still had unequal powers. Its designers were choosing who could observe others, who could interfere and how those privileges were earned.

In a 2017 Essex interview, Bartle described a further ambition: freedom from the social constraints he associated with working-class life in 1970s Britain. This is his later account of the project, not a recorded statement from every early player. He also recalled a division of interests, with Trubshaw drawn toward the world's underlying behaviour and himself toward its content. MUD's identity experiment was built through that collaboration. What a participant could become depended both on imaginative possibility and on the quite specific rules these people wrote.
story_headings: A world that can be changed

old_entry.title: The Oregon Trail
old_entry.subtitle: The classroom as a game space
old_entry.summary: A teaching experiment made decisions, resources and consequences part of a history lesson.
body: Don Rawitsch, Bill Heinemann and Paul Dillenberger created an early Oregon Trail for a Minnesota classroom in 1971. Later versions, associated with the Minnesota Educational Computing Consortium, reached generations of schoolchildren through shared computers.

Food, money, travel and illness became linked systems. Playing could make a lesson memorable, but a simulation also chooses whose experiences to represent. The familiar settler viewpoint is a useful starting point for asking what a historical game leaves outside its frame.

The first version of the game was developed over the course of two weeks for use by Rawitsch in a history unit at Jordan Junior High School in Minneapolis. Despite its popularity with the students, it was deleted from the school district's mainframe computer at the end of the school semester. Rawitsch recreated the game in 1974 for the MECC, which distributed educational software for free in Minnesota and for sale elsewhere, and recalibrated the probabilities of events based on historical journals and diaries for the game's release the following year. After the rise of microcomputers in the 1970s, the MECC released several versions of the game over the next decade for the Apple II, Atari 8-bit computers, and Commodore 64 computers, before redesigning it as a graphical commercial game for the Apple II under the same name in 1985.

The game is the first entry in The Oregon Trail series; games in the series have since been released in many editions by various developers and publishers, many titled The Oregon Trail. The multiple games in the series are often considered to be iterations on the same title, and have collectively sold over 65 million copies and have been inducted into the World Video Game Hall of Fame. The series has also inspired a number of spinoffs such as The Yukon Trail and The Amazon Trail.

The Oregon Trail is a text-based strategy video game in which the player, as the leader of a wagon train, controls a group journeying down the Oregon Trail from Independence, Missouri, to Oregon City, Oregon, in 1847. The player purchases supplies, then plays through about 12 rounds of decision-making, each representing two weeks on the trail. Each round begins with the player being told their current distance along the trail and the date, along with their current supplies. Supplies consist of food, bullets, clothing, miscellaneous supplies, and cash, each given as a number. Players are given the option to hunt for food, and in some rounds to stop at a fort to purchase supplies, and then choose how much food to consume that round. The game closes the round by randomly selecting one or two events and weather conditions. The events include storms damaging supplies, wagons breaking down, and attacks by wild animals or "hostile riders"; weather conditions can slow travel, which can increase the rounds needed to reach Oregon.

old_entry.title: Pong
old_entry.subtitle: Two People Are Enough to Fill a Screen
old_entry.summary: Two paddles and one moving square helped turn electronic play into a public business.
body: Pong is a 1972 sports video game developed and published by Atari, Inc. for arcades. It was created by Allan Alcorn as a training exercise assigned to him by Atari co-founder Nolan Bushnell. Bushnell and Atari co-founder Ted Dabney were so surprised by the quality of Alcorn's work that they decided to manufacture the game. Bushnell based the game's concept on an electronic ping-pong game included on the Magnavox Odyssey, the first home video game console; in response, Magnavox later sued Atari for patent infringement.

Pong is a two-dimensional sports game that simulates table tennis. The player controls an in-game paddle by moving it vertically across the left or right side of the screen. They can compete against another player controlling a second paddle on the opposing side. Players use the paddles to hit a ball back and forth. The goal is for each player to reach eleven points before the opponent; points are earned when one fails to return the ball to the other.

Allan Alcorn builds the first Pong with dedicated electronic circuits, at a time when the microprocessor is not yet the normal tool for creating an arcade video game. The behavior of the ball, paddles, score and video signal therefore comes directly from the hardware. This makes the project especially concrete: every rule must be translated into physical components and connections, without the flexibility of modern software. Alcorn also uses an inexpensive black-and-white television as the prototype display because a dedicated monitor would have cost much more. Pong's visual simplicity is not only an aesthetic choice, but the result of balancing cost, reliability and readability. The game's design almost literally coincides with the machine that produces it, making engineering and rules inseparable.

The prototype is installed at Andy Capp's Tavern in Sunnyvale, where people can try it without needing a manual. The most famous story retold by the Computer History Museum concerns an apparent malfunction: the machine stops accepting games because the coin container is full. The anecdote should be read as evidence of the strong interest generated by the test, not as a scientific measurement of the market. Its value lies in showing a very concrete method. Atari observes that two knobs, a ball and an understandable rule are enough to create a repeatable social practice in a public venue. Public response therefore becomes design and commercial information. Pong quickly demonstrates that an arcade video game can be learned by watching someone else play and can generate continuous turnover between spectators and participants.

Pong can be explained in one sentence, but that does not mean every match is the same. The ball's trajectory and the timing of impact turn paddle position into prediction, while a human opponent introduces variations impossible to program as a simple sequence. The match is readable because there are no superfluous elements: every movement on screen has a function and every mistake produces an immediate consequence. This economy dramatically lowers the barrier to entry and suits a public environment, where the time available to understand what to do must be minimal. Complexity is transferred from the rules to the relationship between two people. In this sense, Pong anticipates a fundamental quality of many competitive games: a few stable rules can generate very different situations when the system places players directly against each other.

Calling Pong the first video game would erase a history that had already begun. Magnavox Odyssey also exists in 1972, a home console commercialized that same year, and other interactive experiments had been developed even earlier. The Computer History Museum itself notes that Odyssey probably influenced Nolan Bushnell. Pong's importance should therefore be sought elsewhere: in its ability to turn an electronic game idea into an arcade product that was highly visible, easy to copy and profitable for a new company. Its fame often simplified collective memory, making the beginning of the entire medium coincide with a single screen. A more precise historical reading does not diminish Pong. On the contrary, it helps explain why this particular project, within an ecosystem already in motion, had commercial and cultural force far greater than its apparent technical simplicity.

After the arcade's success, Atari brings Pong toward the home market. The Computer History Museum reconstructs the work led by Alcorn to concentrate the game into a custom integrated circuit and the later sale to Sears, which in 1975 orders an enormous number of units for the holiday season. This is an industrial transition as well as a technological one. To enter homes, the product needs controlled costs, large-scale manufacturing, national distribution and an object simple enough to connect to a television. The game remains recognizable, but the system supporting it changes. This trajectory helps explain Pong's legacy: not only a set of rules imitated by many competitors, but a model of how an electronic experience can move from an artisanal prototype to an arcade cabinet and finally to a mass-market consumer product.

editorial_features.title: The machine meets its location
editorial_features.summary: A working game still had to survive players, operators and collection day.
body: Ted Dabney's account includes work that rarely fits a game screenshot. He and Nolan Bushnell bought a route of pinball machines, pool tables and other amusements from a Nutting salesman. Collecting those machines' takings helped support them without their old salaries. A location was therefore already a working relationship, not an abstract market. Someone had to own the equipment, place it, collect the money and keep it usable. A new electronic game entered that routine of physical and commercial obligations.

Dabney recalled putting the early Pong prototype into a small cabinet and adapting a laundry-machine coin mechanism. Later machines could go into places on the route. His oral history moves backwards to distinguish that first installation from a subsequent batch of prototypes, a useful warning against treating every remembered number as a production ledger. Testing meant watching an object operate away from its workbench. The cabinet, payment interface and venue mattered alongside the ball on the screen. Failure could come from the container as readily as from the circuit.

Al Alcorn remembered another lesson in the paddle controls. An inexpensive potentiometer wore out after heavy use. Counting coins and estimating the many knob movements within each paid game revealed a much harsher duty cycle than a brief workshop demonstration suggested. The team sought a more durable component. This was feedback expressed through a damaged part rather than a written player survey. A successful attraction demanded more engineering because people kept touching it. The physical gesture that made the game accessible also became a recurring maintenance requirement.

Service habits could cause trouble too. Alcorn recalled early machines with external power supplies returning after operators adjusted the visible voltage control while trying to improve sound or picture. Integrating the supply into the board reduced that opportunity for damage. His explanation connects circuit design with the people expected to maintain a cabinet. The lesson was specific and expensive: supplying a functioning prototype did not guarantee a dependable product. What happened after installation could change the hardware that eventually left the workshop for the next location.

clarity_replaced_playhub_passages.old_body: On November 29, 1972, the Computer History Museum dates Atari's announcement of Pong. The date should not be confused with earlier prototype tests in California bars, nor with the home versions that would arrive years later. Pong began as the first project assigned to Allan Alcorn at the young Atari founded by Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney. On screen are two paddles, a ball and a score: almost nothing, and for that very reason every element must be immediately understandable. The game turns a television into a social space in which two people read trajectories, anticipate rebounds and learn through a few seconds of practice. The commercial success of that simplicity helps Atari grow and makes Pong one of the symbols of the emerging coin-operated video game industry.

clarity_replaced_playhub_passages.old_body: November 29, 1972 is useful precisely because it forces a distinction among the stages of Pong's history. The Computer History Museum records Atari's announcement of the game on this date, while the prototype designed by Allan Alcorn had already been built and tested. An accurate calendar should not turn every anniversary into an implausible day zero. Pong emerged through design, field testing, public response and later commercialization. The announcement belongs to that process and marks the moment when Atari formally presents a product destined to become central to the young company. Separating prototype from announcement makes the history more interesting, because it shows that success does not come from a single isolated intuition: it depends on how a simple technical solution is tested, recognized and turned into industrial activity.

old_entry.title: Atari Video Computer System
old_entry.subtitle: A library in cartridges
old_entry.summary: The console later called the Atari 2600 made a changing software collection part of home life.
body: Atari released its Video Computer System in 1977. Its cartridge library eventually ranged from arcade conversions to original adventures and experiments. Distinctive controllers, a wood-grain front and game boxes turned computer entertainment into a recognisable household product.

Creating for the machine demanded precise control of limited memory and display timing. Its constraints helped produce a visual vocabulary of strong silhouettes, flat colour and repeated patterns that remains readable decades later.

editorial_features.title: Learning the new box
editorial_features.summary: Manuals teach a household to play.
body: The Atari VCS owner's booklet begins before any game can start. Its diagrams address different television antenna connections, explain the TV/Game switch box and show where the controllers belong. The household television was existing equipment with its own fittings and habits. Buying a console did not replace that arrangement; it added another use that had to be connected and later switched away. The drawings turn installation into a sequence a household can follow. Their prominence shows how much instruction belonged outside the game program itself.

Once a cartridge was inserted with the power off, more choices remained. Atari's booklet explains a numbered Game Select display, separate difficulty switches for the two players and a reset switch that starts the chosen game. It sends the owner back to the individual game's instructions for what those settings mean. The console supplied a common vocabulary of controls, while each cartridge interpreted it. A box that could host different games therefore needed a continuing partnership between its physical switches, the screen and the paper placed beside it.

Fairchild's 1976 booklet calls the console programmable, but its opening examples make that word concrete. For the built-in Hockey game, numbered buttons answer on-screen prompts about the game, time limit and speed. An owner can accept defaults or select options before starting. This is programming as the booklet presents it to a player: configuring an activity through a controlled conversation with the machine. It does not mean that every buyer is writing software. The distinction helps recover what a flexible game system actually offered within an ordinary evening.

The Fairchild controller also changes meaning with the activity. In Hockey, the booklet maps movement, twisting and vertical knob action to players and goalie, with diagrams explaining how these motions can combine. Optional Videocart software extends the system beyond its built-in Hockey and Tennis. The hand stays around the same object while the instructions change what that object does. Comparing the two manufacturers' booklets makes interchangeability tangible: a continuing household device, new rules arriving with software, and people learning how to connect the two.
